title: Improving students’ reading, comprehension, and reading motivation through texts generated from their prompts using ChatGPT-4: a mixed-method study
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether student-generated prompts, when used with ChatGPT-4 to create reading texts, questions, and visuals, can improve elementary students’ reading performance, comprehension, and motivation. The study is motivated by the need to strengthen literacy in the elementary years and by interest in whether generative AI can support reading instruction in ways that remain aligned with traditional teaching practices.

The intervention was a ChatGPT-4-supported literacy program in which 4th-grade students proposed prompts, the model generated texts and related activities, and students then read and discussed the materials in class. The quantitative component used a Solomon four-group experimental design, while the qualitative component used a case study approach based on student interviews. The study took place in two public primary schools in Bursa, Türkiye, with 106 students in the quantitative sample and 20 students in the qualitative follow-up.

Results indicated that the experimental groups outperformed the control groups on reading errors, comprehension, and reading motivation, with statistically significant differences and large effect sizes. Qualitative feedback suggested that students found the AI-generated materials engaging and motivating, and that the prompt-based process helped them feel active in text creation. The author concludes that ChatGPT-4 can be integrated into primary reading instruction as a supportive tool, particularly for generating texts that match student interests and support comprehension practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot/large language model system that produces text in response to prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used with 4th-grade students to generate reading texts, comprehension questions, and visuals from students' own prompts for reading instruction and activities.

findings.finding_summary: In the Solomon four-group experiment with 4th-grade students (n=105), the experimental groups outperformed the control groups on post-test reading errors. The paper reports statistically significant differences favoring the experimental groups and an effect size of η²=0.289 for reading error count.
findings.measure: Post-test reading error count from the Error Analysis Inventory

findings.finding_summary: In the same study (n=105), the experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control groups on post-test reading comprehension. The paper reports a large effect size of η²=0.399 for comprehension score.
findings.measure: Post-test comprehension score from open-ended questions in the Error Analysis Inventory

findings.finding_summary: The experimental groups also showed statistically significant gains over the control groups in post-test reading motivation. The paper reports an effect size of η²=0.16, which is interpreted in the article as a large/meaningful effect.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method study with a Solomon four-group experimental component and qualitative interviews, but it is not presented as a fully controlled RCT with all credibility criteria documented in the excerpt. The overall design supports causal inference better than purely correlational work, but the mixed-method nature and some reporting limitations keep it in the yellow tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are large for reading error count (η²=0.289) and comprehension (η²=0.399), and the motivation effect is also substantial at η²=0.16. These are well above the blue-tier threshold for medium/large impact.
